text: You're given daily stock prices. You can buy and sell as many times as you like, but you must sell before buying again — and after you sell, you cannot buy the next day. That's a one-day cooldown. Maximize profit.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I hold at most one share at a time, the cooldown applies only after a sell, not after a buy, and it's exactly one day. Can I buy and sell on the same day?
All correct. Same-day buy-then-sell is pointless — zero profit — so don't worry about it. There are up to five thousand days of prices.

Let me run through the example. One, two, three, zero, two gives three: buy at one, sell at two, cool down through day two, buy at zero, sell at two. Total three. And notice — without the cooldown I'd buy at one, sell at three, buy at zero, sell at two, for four. So the cooldown genuinely costs a point here; it's not a decoration.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. Greedy won't work — summing every positive price rise is the no-cooldown answer, and it overshoots, as I just showed. So it's DP, and the question is what the state is. The day alone is not enough: two days with the same index and the same cash can have different futures, depending on whether I'm holding, and whether I just sold. This problem reminds me of a state machine DP — a few parallel states per day instead of one value. At the end of each day I'm in exactly one of three states: hold, holding a share; sold, just sold today, so tomorrow is the cooldown; and rest, no share and did not just sell, so I'm free to buy tomorrow.
Why two different no-share states? Isn't that redundant?

That's exactly where the cooldown lives, so it's worth being precise. The two states can hold the same amount of cash — but they have different legal moves tomorrow. From sold I cannot buy; from rest I can. The general rule I go by: two situations can share a state only if their futures are identical. Same value doesn't matter; same options does. Merging them here would silently delete the cooldown rule. And notice — nothing in my code will count cooldown days. The rule is encoded in the state graph itself, not in a counter.

Here's the plan — three transitions, each looking only at yesterday. One: hold is the max of keeping yesterday's hold, or buying today out of yesterday's rest. Two: sold is yesterday's hold plus today's price. Three: rest is the max of yesterday's rest and yesterday's sold. On day zero, hold is minus the first price and the other two are zero; the answer is the max of sold and rest on the last day. One thing worth flagging: the entire cooldown is one word — hold reads rest, never sold. Yesterday's sale money has to spend a day walking to rest before it can buy anything. And sold has no max, on purpose: sold means I sold today, so there's exactly one way in. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Why exclude hold from the answer?

Hold means I'm still holding a share on the last day — that money is unrealized, and the value already has the purchase cost subtracted. Ending while holding is never better than having sold, since a price is never negative. Including it wouldn't give a wrong answer; it's just never the max.

Three arrays first — they map one to one to the recurrence, and I can print the table to debug. The line that's easy to get wrong is the buy: hold reads yesterday's rest minus today's price, not yesterday's sold. Then, since every state reads only yesterday, the arrays are pure waste — three variables suffice, for constant space. I copy yesterday's three values into prev variables before updating. Linear time, constant space. A single day needs no special case: the loop never runs, and it returns the max of zero and zero, which is zero.
On the hold line of the second version you read reset, not prev reset. Is that a bug?

Good question, and I want to be honest about it — it's correct today, because reset isn't reassigned until the third line, so it still holds yesterday's value. But it's correct by accident of ordering, not by construction, and that's a bad property. Those three lines look order-independent, since they read snapshots. So a future reader moves the reset line to the top. Now hold reads the new reset, which means buying with money I sold yesterday. The cooldown silently disappears, and one, two, three, zero, two returns four instead of three — the no-cooldown answer. So I'd write prev reset there too. If I take snapshots, I should use them everywhere; then the order really doesn't matter.

Let's dry-run one, two, three, zero, two — expected three. Day three is where the cooldown actually bites: hold is the max of minus one, and rest from day two, which is one, minus a price of zero — so one. It buys with rest's money, not sold's two, which looks better but is still frozen. Take that restriction away and hold becomes two, and the answer inflates to four. On the last day sold is three and rest is two, so the answer is three. That matches. Corner cases: a single day returns zero. Strictly falling prices, five, four, three, two, one, also return zero.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — three max operations per day. Space is constant for the variable version. Oh, one more thing — the constant-space trick works only because the cooldown is exactly one day, so everything depends on yesterday. If the cooldown were k days, the buy would have to reach k days back, so I'd keep k days of history. And this whole family of stock problems is one state machine with different rules: with no cooldown, sold and rest merge; a transaction fee goes on the sell edge; a limit on transactions adds a count dimension. The question is always what the rule forces me to remember — the states fall out of that.

Strong pass. Three things stood out. You showed the greedy answer overshoots before committing to DP, which justified the whole approach. You defended the two no-share states with a real principle — same options, not same value — instead of reciting the template. And when I asked about reset on the hold line, you knew your own code was correct by accident and explained the exact reorder that breaks it. Good work.
